public_rationale: Workplace research shows that automation can reduce skill requirements in some jobs, while other changes need not reduce overall skill. That makes part of the proposed mechanism plausible. It does not establish Zitron's more specific claim: an increasing practice of treating labor as unskilled because AI could theoretically perform it, even when output is inadequate. The required causal link remains undocumented.
limitations: The strongest workplace evidence predates the target period.
Actual task simplification differs from managerial devaluation based on a hypothetical substitute.
The claim does not specify how much reclassification would establish the trend.

our_interpretation: Recategorization includes explicit managerial treatment of previously skilled work as requiring little skill; a formal HR classification change is not required.
The proposed cause is perceived AI substitutability, including cases where output is inadequate.
More and more alleges an increasing pattern, not merely one instance of automation.
The context concerns the emerging 2023 generative-AI rollout through publication.
The because and even-if clauses describe the claimed mechanism, not conditions on a future forecast.
criteria.support_condition: Dated corporate statements, classifications or staffing policies show increasing treatment of skilled work as unskilled because of perceived AI substitutability, including documented cases where inadequate output did not prevent that treatment.
criteria.contradiction_condition: Representative evidence testing this mechanism shows that perceived substitutability does not produce the alleged reclassification, or that the observed changes have a different demonstrated cause.
